+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.34.7	mercy with judgment	The same name-proclamation preserves steadfast love and forgiveness yet does not clear guilt; it directly illuminates the commentary's insistence that expansive mercy does not abolish reckoning.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.50.13	meat and blood do not feed God	The psalm asks whether God eats bulls' flesh or drinks goats' blood, a pointed parallel to the commentary's claim that sacrificial meat and blood do not reach God.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.13.15	sacrifice of praise and name	The sacrifice is praise, the verbal fruit that acknowledges God's name; it closely matches the commentary's movement from animal material to piety and named praise.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.13.16	sacrifice as doing good	The text calls doing good and sharing sacrifices pleasing to God, giving a Christian counterpart to the commentary's claim that the moral disposition of offerers, not animal flesh, reaches God.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.20.24	altar and remembered name	At the authorized altar God makes his name remembered, receives offerings, and blesses; this joins the commentary's name-over-sacrifice with its claim that the name changes the ritual relation.
+strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Exod.34.15	food from a rival sacrifice	Israel is warned that joining a neighboring people's sacrifice and eating it draws one into their gods; this closely parallels food's altered status through a name, though the Torah narrates covenantal entanglement rather than the Qur'anic slaughter formula.
+strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:1Cor.10.20	sacrifice's recipient	Paul says pagan sacrifices are offered to demons and not to God, making the recipient decisive for communion just as the commentary makes the name over meat decisive for its ritual status.
+strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Gen.7.1	Noah's household in ark	Genesis commands Noah and all his household into the ark because of Noah's righteousness; beside the commentary's 11:45-46, its inclusion of the household sharpens the Qur'anic denial that descent alone secures Noah's son.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.8.1	God remembers ark passengers	God remembers Noah, every beast, and the livestock in the ark and begins to subdue the flood; this is the Biblical rescue scene beside the commentary's journey enclosed by divine mercy.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:1Pet.3.20	Noah saved through water	First Peter identifies the few preserved through the floodwaters, keeping the ark's protected passage central to its retelling of Noah.
+strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:1Pet.3.21	ark water reread as baptism	The author makes the floodwater correspond to baptism; this Christian rereading changes the commentary's ark-as-mercy enclosure into a rite that saves through Christ's resurrection.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	Wisdom of Solomon 10:4	Noah steered by wood	Wisdom depicts Wisdom saving the righteous man by steering him on a small piece of wood when the earth flooded, a Jewish retelling of the voyage whose movement the commentary places under God's name.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.32.19	Moses returns angry to calf	Moses comes down, sees the calf and dancing, burns with anger, and throws the tablets; the scene directly accompanies the commentary's Musa, Harun, calf, anger, and later mercy sequence.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.32.14	wrath turns from destruction	YHWH relents from the announced disaster after Moses' intercession. It gives the Biblical side of the commentary's movement from anger at the calf toward mercy.
+strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.103.13	Hebrew r-ḥ-m directed to children	The psalm uses the Hebrew r-ḥ-m verb for a father's compassion to children and then YHWH's compassion to those who fear him, closely matching the commentary's Rahim as mercy directed toward particular recipients.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.145.9	mercy over all creation	YHWH's goodness is said to reach all and his compassion all he has made, a close textual partner for the commentary's Rahman as overflowing mercy that encompasses everything.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jonah.4.2	mercy reaches outsiders	Jonah invokes God's gracious, compassionate, slow-to-anger character as the reason Nineveh may be spared; it makes the scope and scandal of divine mercy concrete alongside the commentary's universal Rahman.
+strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Isa.46.3	Hebrew reḥem and divine carrying	The verse uses Hebrew reḥem, cognate with the commentary's rahim, while God describes bearing Israel from the womb onward; it tightly joins womb imagery to sustaining divine care.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.49.15	mother's womb and compassion	Isaiah asks whether a mother can fail to have compassion for her womb-born child, then contrasts that possibility with God's unfailing remembrance. It gives a direct Biblical analogue for mercy's maternal, protective image.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.139.13	God forms within womb	The psalm credits God with forming the speaker's inward parts and knitting him in his mother's womb, matching the commentary's claim that the one named in 1:1 forms persons in wombs.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.58.7	mercy toward own flesh	True worship includes feeding the hungry, housing the homeless, clothing the naked, and not hiding from one's own flesh; it joins the commentary's kinship-from-one-womb and mercy-as-concrete-good.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.10.33	compassion becomes aid	The Samaritan is moved with compassion and immediately tends the vulnerable stranger. This gives narrative form to the commentary's claim that rahma is tenderness that entails beneficent action.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.6.36	mercy patterned on God	Jesus commands disciples to be merciful as their Father is merciful, an explicit movement from divine mercy to directed human practice like the commentary's Rahim.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ruth.2.12	refuge under God's wings	Boaz blesses Ruth for seeking refuge beneath YHWH's wings; it offers a concrete Biblical image for the commentary's mercy as a place one enters for protection.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.23.37	mercy shelters as a bird	Jesus likens his desired gathering of Jerusalem to a hen gathering chicks under wings. The protective enclosure closely meets the commentary's womb-house image, while the refusal adds its boundary.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.4.16	mercy and help in need	Approaching the divine throne yields mercy and grace for timely help, directly meeting the commentary's final pairing of Rahman with the one from whom help is sought.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.121.2	help from the maker	The psalmist's help comes from YHWH, maker of heaven and earth; it is a concise Biblical partner for the commentary's musta'an and nasta'in connection.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Isa.42.8	unique divine name	YHWH declares "that is my name" and refuses his glory to another, a direct companion to the commentary's no-namesake claim and its empty rival names.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Isa.40.25	no one comparable to God	The prophet asks to whom God can be compared or likened. Its question closely meets the commentary's rhetorical question whether any being can carry God's name as an equal.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.3.15	name given for remembrance	God identifies the divine name as the name to be remembered through generations; this provides a Biblical scene where divine self-naming makes invocation and memory possible.
+strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Deut.6.4	Arabic ilah and Hebrew elohim	The commentary's ilah/Allah explanation meets Hebrew elohenu, a Semitic cognate in Israel's confession that YHWH is one; the verse links cognate divine terminology to exclusive worship.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.23.13	no utterance of other gods' names	The command forbids mentioning other gods' names. It supplies a Torah counterpart to the commentary's contrast between Allah's name and names that lack divine warrant.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:1Cor.8.4	idols and the one God	Paul says an idol has no real existence and that there is no God but one; it is a close Christian articulation of the commentary's empty names and single object of worship.
+strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Gen.11.4	Hebrew shem and Arabic ism, exalted name	Babel's builders seek to make a shem for themselves while raising a tower; Hebrew shem is cognate with Arabic ism, and the verse makes name, height, reputation, and self-exaltation a single scene.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.12.2	God makes a name great	God promises Abram a great name, a close narrative counterpart to the commentary's raising of remembrance as a divine gift rather than self-made reputation.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:2Sam.7.9	God grants David a great name	God says he has made David's name great among the great ones of the earth. This supplies another named person whose elevated remembrance is bestowed rather than merely claimed.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.8.1	name above earth and heavens	The psalm calls YHWH's name majestic in all the earth and sets his splendor above the heavens, directly pairing exalted name with the commentary's horizon-and-sky imagery.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.104.19	moon marks appointed times	The moon is made for appointed times, a specific Biblical counterpart to the commentary's newly visible crescent as a temporal sign.
+strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Deut.4.19	sun, moon, and stars not worshiped	The Torah forbids being drawn into worshiping the celestial host. It directly sits beside the commentary's images of moon and sun rising and its warning that a celestial body can be treated as a god.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.2.19	names as knowledge and recognition	God brings animals to the human to see what he will call them, and their names establish recognition. It is a Biblical counterpart to the commentary's claim that learned names open knowledge.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.44.5	name inscribed as belonging	One person writes "YHWH's" on his hand and takes Israel's name; name and written sign together mark membership, closely paralleling the commentary's name as an owner-identifying brand.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.9.4	forehead mark distinguishes protected people	A mark is placed on the foreheads of those grieving Jerusalem's abominations before judgment. It makes the commentary's visible sign of allegiance an instrument of recognition and protection.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.7.3	sealed servants before judgment	God's servants are sealed on their foreheads before destructive judgment proceeds, a Christian development of the commentary's mark that identifies whose people are protected.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.14.1	divine names on foreheads	The Lamb's followers bear his name and the Father's name on their foreheads; this is an especially direct Christian image of a name functioning as a public mark of whose people they are.
+strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Rev.13.17	another name as economic mark	The beast's mark or name controls buying and selling. It offers a contrary apocalyptic development of the commentary's mark/name motif: a rival name brands allegiance and changes permitted commerce.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.30.32	marked livestock and ownership	Jacob's agreement assigns livestock by visible color markings, so a distinguishable animal becomes identifiable as his wage. This gives a concrete Biblical parallel to the commentary's branded camel known by its owner.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.19.12	oath by the divine name	False swearing by YHWH's name profanes it, closely matching the commentary's treatment of the name as both an invoked refuge and a witness in an oath.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.116.4	calling on the name in distress	The psalmist calls on YHWH's name for deliverance, giving a Biblical prayer-act to place beside the commentary's name that attaches the speaker to its owner.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.10.13	calling on Lord's name for salvation	Paul makes calling on the Lord's name the stated means of salvation, an explicit Christian use of divine-name invocation as refuge.
+strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Luke.1.35	womb and divine Sonship	The annunciation says Mary's child will be called Son of God. It directly contrasts with the commentary's use of womb-rooted Rahman while denying that Rahman takes a child.
+strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:John.3.16	God gives the unique Son	John's soteriological claim that God gives the only Son gives a central Christian form of the proposition the commentary rejects when it says the merciful divine name does not entail divine childbearing.
+strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Matt.28.19	single baptismal name with Father, Son, Spirit	The baptismal command places Father, Son, and Holy Spirit under the name; beside the commentary's exclusive names of Allah and Rahman and denial of childship, its different name theology is the point.
+strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Phil.2.9	Jesus given the name above every name	Philippians says God grants Jesus the name above every name. It is a Christian reconfiguration of exalted name that must be read beside the commentary's insistence that no one can bear or rival God's name.
+strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Ps.2.7	royal son language	The enthronement psalm calls the king God's son on the day of decree; as royal or adoptive language rather than a birth narrative, it clarifies one Jewish background whose terminology differs from the commentary's categorical denial of divine child-taking.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mic.6.8	justice and steadfast love over ritual display	Micah answers sacrificial excess with doing justice, loving steadfast love, and walking humbly with God. It closely parallels the commentary's movement from animal matter to the worshiper's moral posture.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.2.13	mercy and judgment	James says judgment without mercy falls on one who did not show mercy, while mercy triumphs over judgment; this gives a focused Christian counterpart to the commentary's mercy and reckoning tension.
+strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:1Cor.10.7	golden calf reread as church warning	Paul quotes the calf episode to warn Corinthian believers against idolatry. This Christian reuse makes the commentary's Musa-and-calf scene an ongoing warning about rival worship.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	2 Maccabees 7:22	Creator forms life in the mother's womb	The mother tells her sons that God, not she, gave them life and ordered their elements in her womb. This Jewish text closely accompanies the commentary's divine formation and sustenance within rahim.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Esth.3.12	letter written in a ruler's name	The royal order is written in the king's name and sealed with his signet; like the commentary's Solomon letter, sender, authority, and visible mark frame a document before its command is acted upon.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.40.22	heavens as tent-like covering	God stretches out the heavens like a curtain and spreads them as a tent. This is a specific Biblical meeting with the commentary's sky as the roof and shelter above an inhabited house.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.16.9	human plan and divine direction	A person plans a path, but YHWH directs the step. It is a concise Hebrew Bible analogue to the commentary's claim that an intended future act must remain tied to God's will.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.55.10	rain makes earth sprout	Divine rain gives seed and bread by making earth sprout. It specifically meets the commentary's secondary sky-cloud-water-vegetation image, though it does not make that image a theory of names.
+medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.5.45	rain falls beyond moral boundaries	Jesus says the Father gives sun and rain to both righteous and unrighteous. This is a plausible Christian meeting with the commentary's rain as mercy and Rahman's wide reach.
+medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Berakhot 35a	blessing before benefit and divine ownership	The Talmud treats benefit from the world without a blessing as misappropriating what belongs to the Holy One. It gives a Jewish rationale for the commentary's claim that naming God over food changes its relation to the eater.
+medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Avot 2:12	all deeds for the sake of Heaven	The maxim that all one's deeds should be for the sake of Heaven offers a Jewish ethical analogue to the commentary's ellipsis, where whatever act follows is placed under God's name.
+medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Babylonian Talmud Niddah 30b	fetus in a protected and taught womb	The passage imagines the fetus within the womb under divine care and instruction before birth. It develops the commentary's rahim as a sustaining interior home, though through rabbinic imagination rather than the Qur'anic wordplay.
+medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	Didache 10:2	meal thanksgiving for the holy name	The post-meal prayer thanks the holy Father for the holy name made to dwell in believers' hearts. It provides an early Christian liturgical parallel for placing food and thanksgiving under a divine name.
+medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church 6	Noah's ark as Church	Cyprian argues from Noah's ark that salvation is not found outside the Church. This makes an ecclesial boundary out of the commentary's ark-as-protective-mercy image.
*** End Patch`;
const r = await tools.apply_patch(patch);
text(JSON.stringify(r));

+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.3.16	pain in carrying and giving birth	The woman's pain in childbearing gives a Biblical counterpart to the commentary's insistence that the womb that bears and nourishes also bears the cost of birth.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.25.25	kinsman redeems an impoverished relative	A nearest relative is charged to redeem a brother's land when he becomes poor. This gives legal concreteness to the commentary's move from common womb to obligations of kinship.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Hos.11.8	compassion restrains anger	God's compassion is stirred while anger against Ephraim is held back. It closely accompanies the commentary's Rahman/Rahim and wrath tension, especially its calf scene in which anger turns toward mercy.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.11.32	mercy after universal disobedience	Paul says that all have been enclosed in disobedience so that God may have mercy on all. This gives a Christian formulation of mercy's widest scope while retaining an account of disobedience.

+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.17.11	kept in the Father's name	Jesus asks the Father to keep the disciples in the Father's name. It gives a specifically Christian development of the commentary's idea that entry under the divine name is a sphere of preservation.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.32.2	teaching as rain that makes growth	Moses compares his teaching to rain and dew falling on grass and vegetation. It meets the commentary's secondary cloud-water-growth image and its association of divine instruction with life-giving nurture.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.107.30	voyage brought to a desired haven	After the storm is quieted, God brings sailors to their desired haven. This is a concrete Biblical meeting with the commentary's concern for a ship's movement and its safe coming to rest.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.13.9	sign on hand, memorial, and speech	The exodus observance is to be a sign on the hand and a memorial before the eyes so that YHWH's instruction is in the mouth. It brings together visible mark, remembrance, and spoken devotion in a way that complements the commentary's name-as-sign.
+medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Babylonian Talmud Rosh Hashanah 17b	mercy attributes recited as a prayer order	The Talmud portrays God showing Moses the order for invoking the mercy attributes when Israel sins. This makes the Exodus mercy-name formula a repeated liturgical opening, a close Jewish interpretive companion to the recited Fatiha.
+medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 151b	mercy toward creatures and mercy from heaven	The maxim that one who has mercy on creatures receives mercy from Heaven turns divine compassion into a directed human ethic, parallel to the commentary's Rahim as mercy reaching particular vulnerable beings.
+medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 2:8	witnessed appearance of the new moon	The mishnah's procedure for father-and-son witnesses who saw the new moon makes communal testimony depend on the newly visible lunar form. It is a Jewish legal setting for the commentary's rising crescent becoming a recognized sign.
*** End Patch`;
const r = await tools.apply_patch(patch);
text(JSON.stringify(r));
